CLUSTER-AUGMENTED REGRESSION
Baseline vs. Augmented Models
for House Price Prediction
A 5-house worked example: why an omitted Location/Cluster variable
can take a regression from R² = 0.04 to a perfect fit.

text_elements: Five houses, three raw features, and a pre-assigned Cluster label
— a 1-D coordinate (e.g., distance along a corridor)
— predict Price from Size, with and without the cluster
Houses 1–2 sit near L = 1–2 and price low; houses 3–5 sit near L = 8–9 and price much higher — the cluster tracks location, not size.

text_elements: Unsupervised k-means on Location L, run before either regression
Both points sit closer to 1.5 than to the Cluster B centroid — they stay in Group A.
All three points sit closer to 8.5 than to the Cluster A centroid — they stay in Group B.
Since every point is already closer to its own centroid than the other, the assignment is stable on the first iteration — the algorithm converges immediately.

text_elements: Simple linear regression — the cluster label is ignored entirely
This single line assumes every square foot is worth the same $0.175k, no matter where the house is located — it cannot tell a Cluster A house from a Cluster B house of the same size.
slides.full_text:
Step 2 — Baseline Model: Size Only
Simple linear regression — the cluster label is ignored entirely
P̂ = β₀ + β₁·S
Ordinary Least Squares
Mean size  
S̄ = 1100


Mean price  
P̄ = 258



β₁ = Σ(S−S̄)(P−P̄) / Σ(S−S̄)²

    = 7000 / 40000 = 0.175


β₀ = P̄ − β₁·S̄

    = 258 − 0.175(1100) = 65.5
Fitted Baseline Equation
P̂ = 65.5 + 0.175 · S
This single line assumes every square foot is worth the same $0.175k, no matter where the house is located — it cannot tell a Cluster A house from a Cluster B house of the same size.

text_elements: P̂ = 65.5 + 0.175·S applied to all five houses
Residuals are not random: A is always over-predicted, B is always under-predicted.
A systematic sign pattern in the residuals is the signature of an omitted variable — Size alone cannot separate “cheap neighborhood” from “expensive neighborhood.”

Cluster-Augmented Regression

text_elements: Add the cluster as a dummy variable, plus an interaction with Size
Cluster dummy: C = 0 for Cluster A, C = 1 for Cluster B
Shifts the intercept for Cluster B (a fixed $ premium)
Shifts the slope for Cluster B (a different $/sqft rate)
This lets each cluster have its own intercept AND its own price-per-square-foot slope — effectively fitting two separate lines within one model.
slides.full_text:
Step 3 — Augmented Model: Size + Cluster
Add the cluster as a dummy variable, plus an interaction with Size
P̂ = β₀ + β₁·S + β₂·C + β₃·(S×C)
C
Cluster dummy: C = 0 for Cluster A, C = 1 for Cluster B
β₂
Shifts the intercept for Cluster B (a fixed $ premium)
β₃
Shifts the slope for Cluster B (a different $/sqft rate)
This lets each cluster have its own intercept AND its own price-per-square-foot slope — effectively fitting two separate lines within one model.

text_elements:
Baseline vs. Augmented — Takeaways
Baseline
• P̂ = 65.5 + 0.175·S
• Uses Size only
• One universal $/sqft rate
• R² ≈ 0.04
• Residuals show a systematic cluster pattern
Augmented
• P̂ = 0.15·S + 100·C + 0.05·S×C
• Uses Size + Cluster + interaction
• Cluster-specific intercept and slope
• R² = 1.0
• Every prediction matches exactly
Takeaway: the jump from R² ≈ 0.04 to R² = 1.0 shows Location/Cluster was the dominant driver of price — not a minor refinement, but a variable the baseline model could not afford to omit.
